title: Comparative Evaluation of Antioxidant and Immunomodulatory Activities of Carrot (Daucus carota L.) Aerial and Root Parts
content: Carrot (Daucus carota L.) is one of the most widely consumed root vegetables; however, its aerial parts (leaves and stems) are largely discarded as by-products during harvest and remain underutilized. This study aimed to compare the antioxidant and immunomodulatory activities between aerial and underground parts, highlighting the potential of aerial parts as functional materials. Four extracts were prepared: aerial hot-water (AS-W), aerial 50% ethanol (AS-E), underground hot-water (UG-W), and underground 50% ethanol (UG-E). Total phenolic and flavonoid contents and radical scavenging activity were highest in AS-E, followed by AS-W, UG-W, and UG-E. None of the extracts exhibited cytotoxicity in RAW 264.7 cells. Nitric oxide production was enhanced by AS-W and UG-W, whereas under LPS-induced inflammatory conditions, AS-E showed the strongest inhibitory effect. Cytokine analysis is expected to show that hot-water extracts stimulate immune-related cytokine production, while AS-E may suppress it under inflammatory conditions. These findings suggest that both aerial and underground parts possess immunomodulatory properties, with variations depending on the extraction method. Overall, the results indicate that carrot aerial parts, often regarded as by-products, have potential as functional food ingredients.
